idiom_name: tokio::select! racing arrivals against tokio::time::sleep (or std::sync::mpsc::recv_timeout in the sync stack)
implementation_notes: In the async stack the watchman is a select: each iteration awaits either an arrival or a sleep for the silence budget, so the pending future - not a timestamp - is the last-seen state, and the timeout branch is the alarm; tokio::time::sleep and its Instant are monotonic and runtime-driven. The sync stack gets the same semantics with std::sync::mpsc::Receiver::recv_timeout, which turns 'nothing within the budget' into Err(RecvTimeoutError::Timeout) on a dedicated thread. What remains hand-written is the expectation registry and the escalation (alert routing, debounce, repeat-while-silent), typically with tracing or metrics as the alert sink.
pitfalls: tokio::time::sleep must be created and awaited inside the runtime, and blocking std::thread::sleep inside an async task parks a worker thread and stalls every other task on it; use the sync variant only on a dedicated thread.

select! drops the losing branch: a half-consumed receive or a non-cancellation-safe future (e.g. a partially written send) loses data when the timeout arm wins - keep arrivals on a cancellation-safe recv and never pair the deadline with a non-cancellation-safe future.

State that lives only in the task (rather than in a shared AtomicU64 stamp) is lost when the monitor restarts with the process, which re-opens the silence window exactly when a crash-looping service most needs watching.

The first sleep is armed only after the first loop iteration: if no message ever arrives the alarm is correct, but in the std variant recv_timeout's Err(Disconnected) means the producer is gone - a different, usually worse condition than silence and worth its own alert text.
A closed channel makes recv() return None immediately forever: the select spins on the arrival arm and the deadline never fires - match on the closed case explicitly and alarm.

variants.name: std threads with mpsc recv_timeout
variants.implementation_notes: For services without an async runtime: a dedicated monitor thread loops on recv_timeout(budget) and treats RecvTimeoutError::Timeout as silence; Instant::now() provides the monotonic stamp for the alert text, and join/shutdown uses a dedicated control channel or an AtomicBool.
pitfalls: recv_timeout restarts the budget on every message, so a chatty producer hides a stalled consumer that shares the channel - watch the consumer's own progress, not the raw arrival stream.
